title: GA4 Acquisition-Channel and Conversion-Funnel Analysis in BigQuery
goal: Produce an acquisition-channel and conversion-analysis of the GA4 public sample (bigquery-public-data.ga4_obfuscated_sample_ecommerce) in BigQuery: identify which acquisition channels bring the most valuable traffic and where the purchase funnel leaks, deliver validated SQL results (funnel + per-channel comparison), 2-3 written findings, and a saved BigQuery view feeding the Session 2 Looker Studio dashboard.
context:
Every online store spends money and effort getting people to visit, but only a small fraction of visitors ever buy. Two questions decide where a business should focus: where do good visitors come from (acquisition channels — organic search, direct, referrals, ads, etc.), and where do visitors drop off on the way to a purchase (the conversion funnel — from landing on the site, to viewing a product, adding it to the cart, starting checkout, and finally buying). Answering both at once shows not just how many people arrive, but which sources actually turn into sales and at which step the store is losing them — the two things you'd act on to grow revenue.
I'm using Google's public GA4 e-commerce sample because it's real, anonymized web-analytics data of exactly this shape, so the analysis mirrors what a working Data/BI analyst does day to day without touching any private data.
The workflow, in everyday terms: first I decide what to measure and how to group traffic into channels; then I look at the raw data to confirm it contains what I expect (this data is nested and partly anonymized, so assumptions have to be checked, not trusted); then I build a query that counts how many visits reach each funnel step, double-check those numbers against an independent count, and break the funnel down by channel to compare sources. Finally I read the results into a few plain-language findings and save the whole calculation as a reusable "view" — a saved query that always returns fresh results — which becomes the single data source for the dashboard I build in Session 2. Each step hands a checked result to the next, so by the end there's a clear chain from raw data to a dashboard a non-technical stakeholder could read.

nodes.label: Draft the session-grain funnel SQL
nodes.detail: Claude writes the CTE-based query using LOGICAL_OR per stage over the CONCAT session key, flags that ga_session_id needs CAST to STRING before concatenation, and warns of a theoretical key-collision risk from using an empty-string delimiter, leaving the choice to the participant.

Step 6.step_action: Read the funnel and channel outputs to draw 2-3 findings -- the biggest funnel leak, the highest-volume channel, and the highest-quality channel -- pressure-testing each claim against the data caveats before committing it.

nodes.label: Ask for 2-3 pressure-tested findings separating volume from quality
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude to draw 2-3 findings from the funnel and channel results that separate traffic volume from conversion quality, and to pressure-test each against three named caveats: first-touch attribution, self-referral contamination, and obfuscated traffic skewing high.

nodes.label: Draft three pressure-tested findings
nodes.detail: Claude drafts three findings: Referral looks like the best real channel but is likely inflated by self-referral traffic from shop.googlemerchandisestore.com (44.2% of Referral users); the (data deleted) bucket tops every metric but is probably a high-intent population rather than a genuine acquisition channel and should be excluded from budget decisions; and Paid Search underperforms everywhere but on only 148 purchases, and is structurally penalized by first-touch attribution since it likely serves a retargeting role.

nodes.label: Paste and review findings

Step 1.step_action: Fix the business question and lock the funnel stages to real GA4 event names. Write down each KPI as an explicit formula and draft the channel-grouping taxonomy that maps source/medium to named channels.
Step 1.input: Study brief; dataset name; prior GA4/ecommerce knowledge; Claude as a sounding board for KPI and channel definitions.
Step 1.output: A one-page scope note: business question, funnel-stage → event-name map, KPI formulas (sessions, stage conversion %, purchase rate, revenue), and a channel-grouping rule table.
rubrics: Every funnel stage maps to an event name that actually exists in GA4 (not invented)
Each KPI has an unambiguous formula with a stated grain (session vs. user vs. event)
Channel rules are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, with an explicit Direct / unassigned fallback
Scope is small enough to land in a single view feeding one dashboard.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The scope note is complete and internally consistent. session-1 notes.docx fixes the funnel→event map (session_start → view_item → add_to_cart → begin_checkout → purchase), gives every KPI an explicit formula with a stated grain (Sessions = COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id, ga_session_id), stage reach per session, revenue on purchase events, AOV, revenue/session, channel share), and lays out a first-touch channel taxonomy mapping medium → named channel with obfuscation tokens broken out.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: a usable scope note covering all required elements exists.

Step 2.step_action: Confirm what the data actually contains before trusting it: list tables/date span, profile event_name frequencies, inspect nested/repeated fields, verify the UNNEST expression, and decide the attribution source based on what is populated.
Step 2.input: BigQuery access to the dataset; scope note from Step 1; Claude for UNNEST syntax and profiling-query help.
Step 2.output: profiling summary: date range, table count, event_name frequency table, confirmed extraction expressions, chosen attribution field (with reason), and a short data-caveats list.
rubrics: Every field used downstream is confirmed to exist and be populated — nothing assumed
UNNEST expressions return the expected cardinality (one ga_session_id per event row)
The event_name list reconciles with the Step 1 funnel stages
Attribution source is chosen with a documented reason; date range and row counts are recorded.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Strong, evidence-first profiling, step2-q01 confirms 92 daily tables spanning 2020-11-01 → 2021-01-31, step2-q02 gives the full event_name frequency table and reconciles cleanly with the Step 1 funnel (all five stages present: session_start 354,970; view_item 386,068; add_to_cart 58,543; begin_checkout 38,757; purchase 5,692), step2-q03 confirms ga_session_id, medium, source, campaign exist and are populated in event_params, step2-q04 verifies the UNNEST/subquery returns one ga_session_id per event row, step2-q05 chooses traffic_source attribution with the obfuscation tokens (<Other>, (data deleted)) surfaced

goal_achievement.Why or why not: profiling summary with date range, table count, event frequencies, confirmed extraction expressions, chosen attribution field, and obfuscation caveats.

Step 3.step_action: Write the funnel query at session grain: flag per session whether each stage event fired, then aggregate to stage counts and step-to-step conversion, using LOGICAL_OR over event_name per session.
Step 3.input: Verified extraction expressions and confirmed event names from Step 2; Claude to draft the query skeleton.
Step 3.output: A runnable funnel query returning sessions reaching each stage plus overall purchase rate.
rubrics: Session grain is correct (distinct user_pseudo_id + ga_session_id)
Query runs inside sandbox limits thanks to the _TABLE_SUFFIX filter
Stage reach is internally consistent, or any non-nesting (e.g. cart without a recorded view_item) is explicitly noted rather than hidden
Output is a clean stage-count + conversion table, not raw event rows.

ratings.output_quality_reason:
The query is at session grain, uses LOGICAL_OR per stage so a session counts once per stage, is _TABLE_SUFFIX-bounded, and returns a clean stage-count + conversion table (360,129 total sessions → 354,857 start → 77,020 view_item → 15,188 add_to_cart → 11,106 begin_checkout → 4,848 purchase; 1.35% overall). 
Two things hold it back from 5: 
■(a) the session key is built with CONCAT(user_pseudo_id, '', CAST(ga_session_id AS STRING)) — no delimiter, unlike the '-' used in Steps 5/7, a latent collision risk and an inconsistency; 
■(b) total_sessions(360,129) exceeds sessions_session_start (354,857) — ~5,272 sessions have a ga_session_id but no session_start event — which isn't explicitly noted, so Rubric 3's "explicitly noted rather than hidden" is only partly met.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: a runnable funnel query returning stage reach + overall purchase rate.

Step 4.step_action: Run the funnel query, resolve any errors, and validate against independent checks -- reconcile purchase sessions against a direct count of purchase events and distinct transaction_id. Only proceed once discrepancies are explained.
Step 4.input: Draft query from Step 3; BigQuery execution; Claude to debug errors and propose validation checks.
Step 4.output: A validated funnel result set plus a short validation log (checks run, expected vs. actual, resolutions).
rubrics: Query executes cleanly with no silent truncation
At least two independent cross‑checks pass (e.g. purchase count reconciles with distinct transactions)
Any obfuscation / data quirk that affects numbers is documented
Results are reproducible on a second run.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The purchase reconciliation is exactly the right independent cross-check and it decomposes cleanly: 5,692 purchase events → 906 without a usable id (23 NULL + 883 (not set)) → 4,786 valid rows → 4,451 distinct transaction_ids, against 4,848 sessions with a purchase event. The gaps (placeholder ids + ~335 duplicate-fired events + event-vs-session spread) are explained rather than hidden. The funnel totals themselves are deterministic (no ANY_VALUE at this stage), so they reproduce on re-run. (Note: the channel-level non-reproducibility surfaces at Steps 5/7, not here.)

goal_achievement.Why or why not: validated funnel result plus a reconciliation that explains every discrepancy.

Step 5.step_action: Extend the validated funnel to segment by acquisition channel using a CASE grouping on traffic_source.source/medium (user first-touch). Compute per-channel sessions, key stage conversions, purchase rate, and revenue.
Step 5.input: Validated funnel query (Step 4); confirmed attribution field (Step 2); Claude to draft the channel CASE logic and segmented aggregation.
Step 5.output: A per-channel comparison result set (sessions, stage conversions, purchase rate, revenue) plus the channel-grouping SQL.
rubrics: Channel rules are MECE with a working fallback; every session maps to exactly one channel
Metrics are computed at session grain with no double‑counting introduced by UNNEST
(direct) / (none) / (not set) are handled explicitly

Obfuscation tokens (data deleted) and <Other> get their own labelled buckets (not silently dumped into a catch‑all), so the ~20% of scrubbed traffic in this sample is transparent; the Unassigned fallback ends up ~0
Per‑channel totals reconcile back to the un‑segmented funnel from Step 4
Attribution model (first‑touch) is stated so it isn't mistaken for GA4's session default channel grouping.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The segmentation is genuinely MECE — six channels, (none) → Direct, obfuscation tokens (<Other>, (data deleted)) in their own labelled buckets, and Unassigned = 0 (no such row appears), which is the validation signal you wanted. Per-channel sessions sum to 360,129, reconciling exactly to the Step 3/4 funnel total (Rubric 5 ✓). Volume-vs-quality is visible: Organic largest (124,115) but 1.13% purchase rate; Referral 3rd on volume (62,460) but best-converting (1.70%, $78.98 AOV); Paid Search weakest across the board (15,846 / 0.93% / $0.67 rev/session). What keeps it off a 5 is Rubric 6: the model is stated as first-touch, but it's implemented with ANY_VALUE(medium) per user, which (a) isn't strictly first-touch — true first-touch picks the medium at the earliest event_timestamp — and (b) is non-deterministic for multi-medium users, which is the root cause of the Step 5 ↔ Step 7 drift.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: a per-channel comparison (sessions, stage conversions, purchase rate, revenue, AOV) plus the channel CASE logic.

Step 6.step_action: Read the funnel and channel outputs to draw 2-3 findings -- the biggest funnel leak, the highest-volume channel, and the highest-quality channel -- pressure-testing each claim against the data caveats before committing it.
Step 6.input: Validated funnel + channel result sets (Steps 4–5); Claude to sense-check interpretations and phrasing.
Step 6.output: 2–3 written findings, each with its supporting metric, the "so what," and a stated caveat/limitation.
rubrics: Each finding cites a specific number from the validated results.
The volume vs. conversion-quality distinction is explicit (no "biggest = best" conflation).
At least one caveat is named (first-touch attribution, sample obfuscation, or short date window).
No claim reaches beyond what the data supports.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The view compiles at one row per session (session_id, user_pseudo_id, channel, five stage booleans, session_revenue) — dashboard-ready and clearly named (R1, R2 ✓) — and it lives in your own project, not the public dataset (R4 ✓; object expiration not noted). Two partials: R3 — re-running the view does not exactly reproduce Step 5. Totals hold (both = 360,129) but per-channel splits drift (e.g. (data deleted) 20,830 → 20,474; Organic revenue $98,664 → $96,986), because ANY_VALUE(medium) reshuffles multi-medium users between runs. R5 — the findings write-up cites Step 5 figures but doesn't explicitly name vw_channel_funnel as its single source of truth, and because of the drift a few figures (e.g. Referral revenue $83,718 vs the view's $83,004) won't match the view exactly.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: three findings, each with supporting metric, "so what," and a named caveat.

Step 7.step_action: Fold the funnel and channel logic into a single documented view so Looker Studio can aggregate it in Session 2. Create the view in the participant's own project, re-run a sanity query against it, and finalize the write-up.

Findings write‑up names the view as its single source of truth for Session 2.

R5 — the findings write-up cites Step 5 figures but doesn't explicitly name vw_channel_funnel as its single source of truth, and because of the drift a few figures (e.g. Referral revenue $83,718 vs the view's $83,004) won't match the view exactly.
